texts.0: SP, due to a late reading of the leader's turn geometry after the pitch out, did not establish and hold the briefed rejoin angle. texts.2: SP, due to an initial bank that was set slightly outside the required rejoin line, allowed the deviation from the rejoin angle to grow to approximately 15 degrees, between the 10 and 20 degree band. The remainder of the rejoin was flown on angle and no IP input was required.

Corrections to bank were small, promptly applied and stopped on the required line, so the rejoin geometry remained stable all the way to the route position.

SP is expected to set the rejoin line earlier and hold it with smaller residual deviations on subsequent sorties.

error_modes.label: Velocity vector, aspect angle and pursuit curve management

texts.0: SP, due to a perceptual error in judging closure and lateral separation, pointed the velocity vector at the leading aircraft before the leader had stabilized in route. The pursuit curve was flown with an aspect angle and an angle off that produced closure directly toward the leader instead of toward the rejoin line. The IP took control to break the closure and restore lateral separation.
texts.1: SP, due to a perceptual error in reading the angle off during the closure, allowed the velocity vector to remain on the leading aircraft while the leader was still turning. The pursuit curve was corrected toward the rejoin line only after the IP verbally directed the reposition, and the correction came late in the closure. Separation was preserved throughout without any IP input on the controls.
texts.2: SP, due to a lag in interpreting the aspect angle during the first part of the rejoin, briefly flew a pursuit curve that placed the velocity vector inside the required rejoin line. SP recognized the developing angle off without prompting and repositioned the velocity vector ahead of the leader's flight path in time. The remainder of the rejoin was flown on the correct pursuit curve with no IP input.
texts.3: SP kept the velocity vector clear of the leading aircraft until the leader stabilized in route, and flew a pursuit curve consistent with the observed aspect angle and angle off. Closure was controlled by geometry rather than by late power changes, and the rejoin line was maintained throughout.
texts.4: SP read the aspect angle and angle off accurately from the start of the rejoin and flew a pursuit curve that placed the aircraft on the route line with no repositioning required. The velocity vector was never directed at the leading aircraft, and closure was resolved entirely through correct geometry.
texts.marginal: SP kept the velocity vector clear of the leading aircraft and stayed within standards, but the pursuit curve was set slightly inside the required line on more than one occasion and needed adjustment as the aspect angle changed. Separation was never reduced below what the maneuver required. SP is expected to assess angle off earlier so that the pursuit curve is correct from the first bank input.

texts_at.0: SP flew the pursuit curve on the turning rejoin with the aspect angle and angle off talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first turning rejoin at this stage and reading the angle off continuously has not yet formed. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to read the angle off continuously so the correction does not need to be directed without the reminder on the next turning rejoins.

Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to read the angle off continuously so the correction does not need to be directed.

This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to interpret the aspect angle from the first bank input rather than repositioning the vector afterward.
texts_at.3: SP kept the velocity vector clear of the leading aircraft and flew a pursuit curve consistent with the observed aspect angle on three of the four rejoins, the fourth needing a small adjustment after the pursuit curve was set slightly inside the line. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to set that one pursuit curve as accurately as the first three.

The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady pursuit curve and aspect judgment.

Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined pursuit curve and aspect judgment.

error_modes.label: Smoothness and solidity of aircraft control during the rejoin

texts.0: SP, due to over-controlling in both pitch and bank while chasing the rejoin line, did not control the aircraft in a smooth and solid manner. The corrections were large and reversed repeatedly, so the aircraft oscillated about the rejoin line and the closure could no longer be predicted from the wing position. The IP took control to steady the aircraft and complete the rejoin.
texts.1: SP, due to abrupt control inputs applied in response to each perceived deviation, flew the rejoin with repeated corrections that were larger than the errors required. The control technique became smooth only after the IP verbally directed slower and smaller inputs, and the aircraft settled late in the maneuver. No IP control input was necessary.
texts.2: SP, due to a tendency to correct in single large inputs early in the rejoin, produced noticeable pitch and bank excursions about the rejoin line. SP recognized the over-control without prompting, reduced the size of the inputs and completed the closure with smooth and solid handling. The route position was reached under full control with no IP input.
texts.3: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid manner throughout the rejoin, applying small, deliberate pitch and bank inputs and holding each correction until the desired result was achieved. The closure remained predictable to the leader from the start of the maneuver to the route position.
texts.4: SP flew the rejoin with control inputs that were barely perceptible from outside the aircraft, with no over-control and no reversals at any point. The aircraft tracked the rejoin line and settled into route position as a single continuous, stable movement.
texts.marginal: SP kept the aircraft under control within standards but used inputs larger than the corrections called for, particularly in bank during the last part of the closure. The technique remained safe and no assistance was needed, yet the handling was more abrupt than the maneuver required. SP is expected to correct with smaller, held inputs so that the closure appears smooth and solid from the leader's position.

SP is expected to size the correction to the error from the first input without the reminder on the next turning rejoins.

This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the first correction correctly rather than reducing an oversized input afterward.
texts_at.3: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid manner on three of the four rejoins, applying small, deliberate pitch and bank inputs, the fourth needing a slightly larger correction than the rest of the closure. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold that same smooth control on every rejoin that the first three showed.

The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured smoothness and solidity of aircraft control.

Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise smoothness and solidity of aircraft control.

error_modes.label: Approach at leader's altitude and descent to the wing line

texts.0: SP, due to an incorrect sequencing of the rejoin, did not initially approach the leading aircraft at the same altitude and instead began the descent toward the wing line while still well out of position. The aircraft closed from below the leader's plane of motion, where the leader's cross-check of the wingman was degraded and the closure could not be assessed. The IP took control to re-establish the aircraft at the leader's altitude before continuing the rejoin.
texts.1: SP, due to an early commitment to the wing line, started the descent from the leader's altitude before the closure was established. The correct sequence, approach at the same altitude first and descent at the wing's level afterwards, was restored only after the IP directed it verbally, and the rejoin was completed late. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an anticipation of the final position, began to move below the leader's altitude slightly before the wing line was reached. SP identified the premature descent on his/her own, returned to the leader's altitude and then descended at the wing's level as required. The sequence was corrected in time and no IP input was needed.
texts.3: SP approached the leading aircraft at the same altitude, completed the closure in that plane and only then descended at the wing's level to take the route position. The sequence was flown as briefed and the wingman remained visible to the leader throughout the rejoin.
texts.4: SP held the leader's altitude exactly through the entire closure and transitioned to the wing's level with a single unhurried descent at the correct point. The sequence was executed with no intermediate corrections and the route position was taken directly from the wing line.
texts.marginal: SP flew the correct sequence and remained within standards, but the descent at the wing's level was initiated slightly before the closure had fully stabilized on more than one rejoin. The leader's altitude was regained each time without assistance. SP is expected to complete the closure in the leader's plane of motion before starting the descent to the wing line.

texts_at.0: SP flew the approach to route position with the same-altitude-first sequence talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first turning rejoin at this stage and completing the closure at the leader's altitude before starting the descent has not yet formed. SP is expected to complete the closure at the leader's altitude before starting the descent without the reminder on the next turning rejoins.

texts_at.2: SP began to move below the leader's altitude slightly before the wing line was reached because of an anticipation of the final position, then identified the premature descent without prompting, returned to the leader's altitude and descended at the wing's level as required. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to hold the leader's altitude until the wing line is reached rather than anticipating the descent.
texts_at.3: SP approached the leading aircraft at the same altitude before descending at the wing's level on three of the four rejoins, the fourth descent begun a moment before the closure had fully stabilized. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold that one closure to the same standard the first three showed.

The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent sequencing of the approach to route position.
texts_above.3: SP approached the leading aircraft at the same altitude, completed the closure in that plane and only then descended at the wing's level to take the route position, exactly as the sequence was briefed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed sequencing of the approach to route position.
texts_above.4: SP held the leader's altitude exactly through the entire closure and transitioned to the wing's level with a single unhurried descent at the correct point, with no intermediate corrections. error_modes.label: Continuous visual contact with the formation leader

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on the cockpit instruments at the expense of the outside scan, did not continuously keep visual on the formation leader during the turning rejoin. Visual contact was lost while the aircraft was still closing, and the rejoin was continued without the leader in sight. The IP took control and directed the reposition required to regain visual and separation.

texts.2: SP, due to a short absorption in a cockpit indication during the first part of the rejoin, briefly interrupted the visual on the formation leader. SP recognized the interruption without prompting, re-established continuous visual contact and reassessed the leader's turn before closure developed further. Visual contact was never actually lost. SP is expected to keep the leader in sight continuously and to limit instrument references to brief glances during the closure.

error_modes.label: Overshoot recognition, timely call and safe execution

texts.0: SP, due to a lack of assertiveness in voicing a recognized unsafe condition, did not inform the formation leader that an overshoot had become unavoidable and did not execute the Overshoot. The aircraft continued to close on the rejoin line with excess overtake and no separating maneuver was initiated. The IP took control to execute the overshoot safely and restore separation.
texts.1: SP, due to a reluctance to state that the rejoin could not be completed as flown, delayed the overshoot call to the formation leader until the overtake was already excessive. error_modes.label: Turning tactical rejoin per Techniques and Procedures Manual

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient knowledge of the published procedure for the tactical rejoin, did not execute the turning tactical rejoin according to the Techniques and Procedures Manual. The closure was flown into the leader's turn without the prescribed geometry or the required lateral separation for the tactical position. The IP took control to reposition the aircraft and terminate the rejoin.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete recall of the tactical rejoin sequence, flew the turning tactical rejoin with the steps of the Techniques and Procedures Manual out of order. The correct procedure was restored only after the IP verbally directed each step, and the tactical position was taken late. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a hesitation in selecting the correct tactical geometry at the start of the maneuver, began the turning tactical rejoin with a line other than the one prescribed by the Techniques and Procedures Manual. SP recognized the error without prompting, re-established the published geometry and completed the rejoin into the correct tactical position with no IP input.
texts.3: SP executed the turning tactical rejoin according to the Techniques and Procedures Manual, with the prescribed geometry, lateral separation and sequence. The tactical position was taken under control and with continuous visual on the formation leader.
texts.4: SP flew the turning tactical rejoin exactly as published, resolving the closure through correct geometry alone and arriving in the tactical position with no intermediate corrections. The procedure was executed without hesitation and with the leader in sight throughout.
texts.marginal: SP executed the turning tactical rejoin in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual, but the geometry was set with visible hesitation and the tactical position was reached later than the procedure intends. The maneuver was safe and unassisted throughout. SP is expected to apply the published tactical rejoin geometry from the first input so that the position is taken without delay.

texts_at.0: SP flew the turning tactical rejoin with each step of the Techniques and Procedures Manual sequence talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first tactical rejoin at this stage and recalling the tactical rejoin sequence fully has not yet formed. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to recall the tactical rejoin sequence fully without the reminder on the next tactical rejoins.
texts_at.1: SP had the correct procedure restored only after IP verbally directed each step, because the tactical rejoin sequence of the Techniques and Procedures Manual was recalled incompletely. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to recall the tactical rejoin sequence fully rather than needing each step directed.
texts_at.2: SP began the turning tactical rejoin with a line other than the one prescribed because of hesitation in selecting the correct tactical geometry, then recognized the error without prompting, re-established the published geometry and completed the rejoin into the correct tactical position with no IP input. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to select the prescribed geometry on the first input rather than correcting it afterward.
texts_at.3: SP executed the turning tactical rejoin according to the Techniques and Procedures Manual on three of the four occasions, the fourth geometry selected with a moment's hesitation before the published line was followed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to select that one geometry as promptly as the first three.

error_modes.label: Aspect control with the vertical stabilizer reference and bank angle

texts.0: SP did not use the vertical stabilizer position relative to the outside wing as the aspect reference, so the 3 aspect / 30 AA picture was never established. Bank angle was held fixed while the stabilizer drove toward the wingtip, aspect built up unchecked and the rejoin angle exceeded 20 degrees with a large line of sight rate on Number 1. The IP took control to unload the aspect and re-establish the rejoin line.
texts.1: SP read the aspect reference late, recognizing the stabilizer movement toward the outside wingtip only after aspect had already increased. Bank angle was not shallowed to decrease aspect until the IP called for it, and the rejoin angle reached about 20 degrees before the correction took effect. The line of sight rate was arrested with no IP input on the controls.
texts.2: SP allowed the vertical stabilizer to drift off the bisected wing picture without an immediate bank adjustment, so aspect increased and the rejoin angle grew to roughly 15 degrees. SP identified the growing line of sight rate unprompted, shallowed bank to decrease aspect and re-centered the reference line before the critical stage of the rejoin. No IP input was required.
texts.3: SP used the vertical stabilizer bisecting the outside wing as the aspect reference and made small bank adjustments to hold it, keeping the rejoin angle within 10 degrees. Movement of the stabilizer toward the wingtip or wing root was answered with the correct bank change before any line of sight rate developed.
texts.4: SP set the 3 aspect / 30 AA picture on the first bank input and held the vertical stabilizer on the outside wing throughout, with no perceptible line of sight on Number 1. The rejoin angle stayed within a few degrees of the reference line and no aspect correction was needed at any point.
texts.marginal: SP held the aspect reference within standards and kept the rejoin angle inside 10 degrees, but the stabilizer picture was re-centered with repeated bank changes rather than held steady, and a small line of sight rate reappeared twice. SP is expected to answer the first movement of the stabilizer with a single measured bank adjustment so the reference line stays stable.

texts_at.0: SP flew the turning rejoin with the vertical stabilizer aspect reference talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first turning rejoin at this stage and reading the vertical stabilizer reference continuously has not yet formed. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to read the vertical stabilizer reference continuously without the reminder on the next turning rejoins.
texts_at.1: SP held the rejoin angle to about 20 degrees, at the tolerance limit, because the aspect reference was read late and bank angle was not shallowed until IP called for it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to read the vertical stabilizer reference continuously so bank is shallowed without needing it called.
texts_at.2: SP let the rejoin angle grow to roughly 15 degrees, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the vertical stabilizer was allowed to drift off the bisected wing picture without an immediate bank adjustment. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to answer the first movement of the stabilizer with an immediate bank adjustment rather than after the angle has grown.
texts_at.3: SP used the vertical stabilizer as the aspect reference and held the rejoin angle within 10 degrees on three of the four rejoins, the fourth needing a small correction after a bank adjustment applied a beat late. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to answer that one stabilizer movement as promptly as the first three.

texts_above.1: SP held the rejoin angle to about 20 degrees, at the tolerance limit, once bank was shallowed to hold the aspect reference. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP let the rejoin angle grow toward 15 degrees because the vertical stabilizer was allowed to drift off the bisected wing picture, but identified the growing line of sight rate unprompted, shallowed bank to decrease aspect and re-centered the reference line before the critical stage of the rejoin. Answering the first movement of the stabilizer with an immediate bank adjustment, rather than after the angle has grown, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good aspect reference discipline with the vertical stabilizer.
texts_above.3: SP used the vertical stabilizer bisecting the outside wing as the aspect reference and made small bank adjustments to hold it, keeping the rejoin angle within 10 degrees with no line of sight rate developing. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good aspect reference discipline with the vertical stabilizer.
texts_above.4: SP set the 3 aspect / 30 AA picture on the first bank input and held the vertical stabilizer on the outside wing throughout, with no perceptible line of sight on Number 1 at any point. error_modes.label: Recognition of excessive overtake against the directed rejoin airspeed

texts.0: SP did not compare actual airspeed with the directed rejoin airspeed of 180 KIAS, so the excessive overtake was never recognized. Closure was carried far above the 20 to 30 KIAS the rejoin is built on and SP was more than 15 knots fast when reaching route, with the closure still increasing. The IP took control to stop the overtake.
texts.1: SP cross-checked the airspeed indicator against the directed rejoin airspeed only after Number 1 called out the actual airspeed. The excessive overtake was acknowledged late, and SP arrived at route position about 15 knots fast before the closure was finally arrested. Recovery was completed without IP control input.
texts.2: SP was slow to compare actual airspeed with the directed 180 KIAS and let closure build beyond the planned 20 to 30 KIAS during the middle of the rejoin. SP detected the overtake unprompted from the airspeed cross-check, reduced power in time and stabilized in route about 10 knots fast before settling. No IP input was required.
texts.3: SP compared actual airspeed with the directed rejoin airspeed throughout the closure and kept overtake near the planned 20 to 30 KIAS. Airspeed at route position was within 5 knots of Number 1 and no callout of actual airspeed was needed.
texts.4: SP tracked the airspeed indicator against the directed 180 KIAS continuously and bled the initial overtake progressively, arriving co-airspeed with Number 1 with only slight positive closure. Airspeed in route was within a couple of knots and no overtake correction was ever required.
texts.marginal: SP recognized the overtake and stayed within 5 knots at route position, but the airspeed comparison was made in steps rather than continuously and closure twice ran above the planned band before being trimmed back. SP is expected to cross-check actual against directed airspeed early enough that overtake never has to be corrected in a single large power reduction.

texts_at.0: SP flew the closure with the actual-versus-directed airspeed cross-check talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first turning rejoin at this stage and cross-checking actual against directed airspeed continuously has not yet formed. SP is expected to cross-check actual against directed airspeed continuously without the reminder on the next turning rejoins.
texts_at.1: SP arrived at route position about 15 knots fast, at the tolerance limit, because the airspeed indicator was cross-checked against the directed rejoin airspeed only after Number 1 called out the actual airspeed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to cross-check actual against directed airspeed continuously so the overtake is not acknowledged only after a call.
texts_at.2: SP let closure build beyond the planned band and stabilized in route about 10 knots fast, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the comparison of actual airspeed against the directed 180 KIAS was slow during the middle of the rejoin. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to compare actual against directed airspeed earlier in the rejoin rather than during its middle stage.
texts_at.3: SP compared actual airspeed with the directed rejoin airspeed and stayed within 5 knots at route position on three of the four rejoins, the fourth needing a small correction after the comparison ran a beat behind the closure. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold that same cross-check timing on every rejoin that the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP arrived at route position about 15 knots fast, at the tolerance limit, once actual airspeed was cross-checked against the directed value. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.

texts_above.3: SP compared actual airspeed with the directed rejoin airspeed throughout the closure and kept overtake near the planned band, arriving within 5 knots of Number 1 at route position with no callout of actual airspeed needed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed recognition of overtake against directed airspeed.
texts_above.4: SP tracked the airspeed indicator against the directed 180 KIAS continuously and bled the initial overtake progressively, arriving co-airspeed with Number 1 with only slight positive closure. error_modes.label: Power and speed brake sequencing to control closure

texts.0: SP did not sequence power and speed brake as the technique requires, selecting idle before extending the speed brake instead of extending it after power was below 20 percent, with the light in the gear handle, and before idle. With no thrust available to modulate and long spool-up time, closure was not controlled and SP passed route position more than 15 knots fast. The IP took control to stop the closure.
texts.1: SP reduced power to idle first and only then extended the speed brake, missing the window below 20 percent indicated by the light in the gear handle. The IP had to direct the power and speed brake sequence verbally, and airspeed in route was about 15 knots off Number 1 while the engine spooled back up. No IP control input was needed.
texts.2: SP extended the speed brake at the wrong point in the power reduction, so the deceleration was uneven and airspeed diverged about 10 knots from Number 1. SP recognized the closure trend without prompting, retracted the boards and reset power before route position, and the deviation was contained. The remainder of the rejoin was flown without IP input.
texts.3: SP reduced power below 20 percent, confirmed the light in the gear handle and extended the speed brake before selecting idle, so thrust remained available to modulate the closure. Airspeed in route was within 5 knots of Number 1 and no large power change was required.
texts.4: SP timed the speed brake extension precisely inside the band below 20 percent and above idle, then retracted the boards and increased power before matching airspeed so no aft movement developed. Airspeed in route matched Number 1 within a couple of knots with slight positive closure preserved.
texts.marginal: SP used the correct power and speed brake sequence and held airspeed within 5 knots of Number 1, but the boards were retracted slightly late so a small aft drift began before power was restored. SP is expected to advance power before matching airspeed so the closure is stopped without any rearward movement.

texts_at.0: SP flew the power and speed brake sequence with the order of the technique talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first turning rejoin at this stage and extending the speed brake before selecting idle has not yet formed. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to extend the speed brake before selecting idle without the reminder on the next turning rejoins.
texts_at.1: SP passed route position about 15 knots off Number 1, at the tolerance limit, because power was reduced to idle before the speed brake was extended, missing the window below 20 percent, until IP directed the sequence verbally. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to extend the speed brake before selecting idle so power stays available to modulate the closure.
texts_at.2: SP let the airspeed diverge about 10 knots from Number 1, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the speed brake was extended at the wrong point in the power reduction, then recognized the closure trend without prompting, retracted the boards and reset power before route position. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to time the speed brake extension inside the correct power band rather than correcting the resulting divergence afterward.
texts_at.3: SP reduced power below 20 percent and extended the speed brake before selecting idle, holding the airspeed in route within 5 knots of Number 1 on three of the four rejoins, the fourth needing a small correction after the sequence ran a beat off. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold that same sequence timing on every rejoin that the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP passed route position about 15 knots off Number 1, at the tolerance limit, once the power and speed brake sequence was corrected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP let the airspeed diverge about 10 knots from Number 1 because the speed brake was extended at the wrong point in the power reduction, but recognized the closure trend without prompting, retracted the boards and reset power before route position, containing the deviation. Timing the speed brake extension inside the correct power band, rather than correcting the divergence afterward, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid power and speed brake sequencing.
texts_above.3: SP reduced power below 20 percent, confirmed the light in the gear handle and extended the speed brake before selecting idle, so thrust remained available to modulate the closure and airspeed in route stayed within 5 knots of Number 1. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed power and speed brake sequencing.
texts_above.4: SP timed the speed brake extension precisely inside the band below 20 percent and above idle, then retracted the boards and increased power before matching airspeed so no aft movement developed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding power and speed brake sequencing.

error_modes.label: Bank and overtake monitoring in the critical stage inside 500 feet

texts.0: SP did not monitor bank and overtake closely during the last few hundred feet, so aspect and closure were not under control when the critical stage of the rejoin began at approximately 500 feet. Lateral and vertical separation were given up before the closure rate was stabilized and the rejoin angle was more than 20 degrees off with Number 1 filling the canopy. The IP took control to arrest the closure.
texts.1: SP relaxed the cross-check of bank and overtake inside 500 feet and began moving forward onto the fingertip reference line before the closure rate was under control. The IP verbally directed the bank and power correction, and the rejoin angle reached about 20 degrees before separation was re-established. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP let attention settle on the fingertip references as they became visible inside 300 to 500 feet and briefly stopped monitoring bank and overtake, allowing the rejoin angle to open to roughly 15 degrees. SP restored the cross-check unprompted, corrected bank and closure and held lateral separation until stabilized in route. No IP input was needed.
texts.3: SP monitored bank and overtake throughout the critical stage inside 500 feet and maintained lateral and vertical separation until the closure rate was stabilized in route. The rejoin angle stayed within 10 degrees while the fingertip references were acquired.
texts.4: SP kept the bank and overtake cross-check continuous through the critical stage, so the transition from the rejoin line to the fingertip references inside 300 to 500 feet produced no change in aspect or closure. The rejoin angle held within a few degrees and separation was never in question.
texts.marginal: SP maintained separation and stayed inside 10 degrees of the rejoin angle, but the bank and overtake cross-check thinned noticeably once the fingertip references appeared and closure had to be trimmed twice in the last few hundred feet. SP is expected to keep monitoring bank and overtake all the way to route position rather than transferring attention to the close references early.

texts_at.0: SP flew the critical stage of the rejoin with the bank and overtake cross-check talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first turning rejoin at this stage and keeping the bank and overtake cross-check running all the way to route position has not yet formed. texts_at.2: SP let the rejoin angle open to roughly 15 degrees, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because attention settled on the fingertip references as they became visible and briefly stopped monitoring bank and overtake, then restored the cross-check unprompted, corrected bank and closure and held lateral separation until stabilized in route. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep the bank and overtake cross-check running as the fingertip references appear rather than transferring attention away from it.
texts_at.3: SP monitored bank and overtake through the critical stage inside 500 feet and stayed within 10 degrees of the rejoin angle on three of the four rejoins, the fourth needing a small correction after the cross-check thinned briefly. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold that same monitoring on every rejoin that the first three showed.

Keeping the bank and overtake cross-check running as the fingertip references appear, rather than transferring attention away from it, would close that margin further. texts_above.3: SP monitored bank and overtake throughout the critical stage inside 500 feet and maintained lateral and vertical separation until the closure rate was stabilized in route, with the rejoin angle held within 10 degrees while the fingertip references were acquired. error_modes.label: Unbriefed rejoin to the outside of the turn and nose-tail separation when crossing

texts.0: SP rejoined to the outside of the turn toward the number 3 position without it having been pre-briefed or directed, contrary to the normal two-ship rejoin to the inside. The cross under Number 1 was flown without the required nose-tail separation and with insufficient closure to complete the move outside the turn circle. The IP took control to reposition the aircraft.
texts.1: SP began the rejoin toward the outside of the turn although the brief called for a rejoin to the inside, and continued until the IP verbally directed the correction. The initial portion was flown correctly but the cross below and behind Number 1 was started with marginal nose-tail separation, and the rejoin angle reached about 20 degrees during the reposition. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP set up for the outside of the turn without a brief or a direction from Number 1, then recognized the error unprompted before crossing the 6 o'clock and re-established the rejoin to the inside. The correction opened the rejoin angle to roughly 15 degrees before the line was regained, and the rejoin was completed with no IP input.
texts.3: SP rejoined to the inside of the turn as briefed, and when the outside position was directed flew the initial portion identically to an inside rejoin, then crossed below and behind Number 1 with at least nose-tail separation. Positive closure of about 10 to 15 knots was preserved for the move outside and the rejoin angle stayed within 10 degrees.
texts.4: SP flew the rejoin exactly as briefed and directed, crossing below and behind Number 1 with clear nose-tail separation and holding the closure needed to get outside the turn circle without a power correction. texts_at.2: SP set up for the outside of the turn without a brief or a direction from Number 1, opening the rejoin angle to roughly 15 degrees before crossing the 6 o'clock, then recognized the error unprompted and re-established the rejoin to the inside before the line was regained. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section.
